column4: The source section labels ض ل ل branch B002 as hiding and disappearing, and cites this wording: ضَلَلْنَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ. Here resurrection-deniers imagine becoming lost in the earth, making bodily disappearance the premise of their denial.

The source section labels ض ل ل branch B004 with the dictionary sense “forget.” This witness rule uses أَن تَضِلَّ for a woman’s lapse of memory and pairs it with a second witness’s reminder, so what slips from memory is restored by speech.
The source section glosses the root of ضحى as coming out into the sun and open view. Moses chooses ضُحًى for the people’s public gathering, placing the contest in daylight where it can be seen.
The source section glosses the root of فَحَدِّثْ as opening or bringing forth. Here the earth تُحَدِّثُ its أخبار, so the ground that covered what was buried becomes the speaker of its news.

The section compares its movement from what was unknown to what is told with this address to the Prophet: God relates the best narrative and says he had been among the unaware before it. The story makes revelation the passage from unknowing into recitation.

The source section defines حديث as speech that reaches a hearer and حَدَّثَ as bringing something out. This verse calls a confidence حديث, then narrates its disclosure to another wife, God making it known to the Prophet, and his revealing part of it.

The section moves from a hidden or missed thing to a found blessing that is spoken of. Solomon sees the distant throne placed before him and calls it a favor from his Lord, explicitly turning discovery into recognition of divine favor.

The section’s covered-to-found movement meets a literal hidden provision: treasure lies beneath a wall for two orphan boys, protected until they mature and can extract it. The explanation identifies the concealed good as mercy from their Lord.

The source section describes finding by perception and the later telling of a favor. Zakariya repeatedly وَجَدَ provisions with Mary, asks where they came from, and she answers that they are from Allah; discovery leads to attribution.

The section joins concealment, finding, and telling. In Joseph’s story a water-drawer lowers a bucket into the well, announces “good news,” finds a boy, and the caravan then hides him as merchandise; the same scene moves from concealment to discovery and back to concealment.

The section’s lost-in-water image meets the fish that disappears into the sea as Moses and his companion reach the meeting of the seas; the verse also says they forgot it. This gives disappearance, water, and forgetting one concrete scene.

The section says a fixed use of ض ل ل carries the sense “forget.” The companion now reports that they forgot the fish and that Satan made him forget to mention it, turning the vanished fish into a spoken recovery of the missed sign.

Moses recognizes the fish’s disappearance as the sign they sought and retraces their steps. This continuation completes the cited fish episode by showing how what vanished becomes findable through remembered testimony.

The section says وَجَدَ can mean noticing or finding through perception and reason. After returning to the site, Moses وَجَدَ a servant of God endowed with mercy and knowledge, a hidden source of guidance he had not known.
After finding the knowledgeable servant, Moses asks whether he may follow him and learn from what he has been taught. The verse completes the discovery with an explicit request for guidance.
Yusuf sees a dream and tells it to his father. This is a specific passage from an inward, unseen experience to narration, matching the section’s move from what is covered to what is said.

The section says the Lord’s favor should be told openly; Jacob instead tells Yusuf not to disclose his dream to his brothers because they may plot against him. The contrast marks a case where keeping what was seen under cover protects the speaker.

The source section notes the secondary word حديث and its relation to what reaches a hearer. This verse says Yusuf will be taught the interpretation of الأحاديث and that God will complete His favor upon him, joining hidden dreams, their interpretation, and bestowed favor.

The source section notes that حديث can name more than ordinary speech. In this verse Joseph is established in the land and taught the interpretation of الأحاديث, so the same term covers knowledge whose meaning must be disclosed.

The section commands the Prophet to tell of his Lord’s favor. Joseph’s closing prayer names what God gave him and thanks Him for teaching him the interpretation of الأحاديث, combining attributed blessing with the section’s secondary dream-and-event sense.
The source section defines finding through the senses. Jacob says he senses Joseph’s scent, إِنِّى لَأَجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ, recognizing the absent one through smell before the news arrives.

The source section’s hidden-to-found movement appears when the bearer of good news arrives with Joseph’s shirt: Jacob’s sight returns after it is placed on his face. What was lost to perception becomes visible again through a sign.

The source section says وَجَدَ can mean noticing through the senses. The hoopoe reports that he found the queen and her people prostrating to the sun, making an observed scene the basis of a message that exposes what had been hidden from Solomon.

The source section describes finding through perception. Dhu al-Qarnayn reaches the setting of the sun and وَجَدَهَا apparently setting in a muddy spring, a narrated sight that makes the perceiver’s standpoint part of what is found.

The source section opposes covering with appearing in the sun. At the sunrise, Dhu al-Qarnayn finds a people with no shelter from it; the verse presents exposure to daylight as the boundary opposite concealment.
The source section says night is a covering and describes finding by sight. In Abraham’s sequence, night covers him and he sees a star; the covered sky becomes the setting for an observed object.

The moon appears in the same sequence, and Abraham says that without his Lord’s guidance he would be among the people astray. The verse joins seeing what appears with the section’s paired ideas of lostness and guidance.

The sequence continues with Abraham seeing the rising sun, the largest of the three lights, then rejecting it when it sets. This contributes the daylight counterpart to the star and moon observations in 6:76–77.

After the star, moon, and sun set, Abraham turns his face to the Creator of the heavens and earth. This resolution completes the neighboring scene of sight and guidance by naming the direction he has found.
The source section explains ضحى as emergence into open sunlight. This verse says God darkened the night and brought out its ضُحَىٰ, a direct image of what was covered becoming visible.
The source section calls night a covering beneath which things are unseen. This oath names the night when it covers, directly staging that side of the image.
The verse immediately sets out the day as it appears, giving the open and visible counterpart to the source section’s covered night.
The source section opposes what is covered to what comes into view. This oath describes the day as it reveals the sun, a close parallel to the image’s emergence into light.
The next oath describes night as it covers the sun, completing the day-and-night reversal that the section reads through concealment and appearance.
The source section calls night a covering. This verse names the night as لباس, a garment, making the concealing function explicit.
The next verse makes day a means of livelihood, supplying the exposed, active counterpart to the night garment in 78:10.
The verse calls night a garment and sleep rest, then makes day a time of spreading out. It links the source section’s covering image to the different activity revealed in daylight.
The verse describes God wrapping night over day and day over night. Its reversible covering gives the section’s night-and-day opposition a recurring, two-way movement.

The verse says daylight is stripped from night and people are suddenly in darkness. This makes the boundary between appearing and being covered an action, matching the section’s movement between hidden and exposed.

The verse makes night dark and day illuminating so people can seek their Lord’s bounty and reckon time. It connects concealment and visibility with the section’s movement from hidden provision to recognition.
The verse assigns rest to night and sight to day. That is a concrete functional contrast between what the section calls covered and what is open to view.

The section says night hides what is underneath its cover. This sea is layered in darkness, and a person can scarcely see his own hand; it gives a concrete scene of sight failing under overlapping cover.

The source section’s dictionary image is water disappearing into milk. This verse gives the boundary case of two waters meeting while a barrier keeps them apart, clarifying the difference between mixture and separation.
The two seas are released and meet, echoing the source section’s image of one liquid entering another; the next verse’s barrier makes the contrast explicit.
The neighboring verse supplies the boundary between the two meeting seas: a barrier they do not cross. It completes the contrast with the source section’s water that disappears within milk.

The source section labels ض ل ل branch B002 as hiding or disappearing. Here what the idolaters invented has vanished from them at judgment, a different scene that uses disappearance to expose the absence of their supposed protectors.

The source section’s B002 sense is something hidden or gone from sight. At the gathering, what people falsely invented disappears from them, so the verse makes loss visible when each soul faces its deeds.
The source section links ض ل ل with disappearance. This verse calls its speakers losers because what they invented has strayed from them, portraying false objects of trust as gone when needed.

The source section’s B002 dictionary sense includes what has gone missing. Here the partners people invented disappear from them when they surrender to God, making the loss a public exposure of their claims.
The source section’s B002 sense is hiddenness or disappearance. This verse says the truth becomes clear and the inventions they relied on vanish, placing disclosure beside the disappearance.
The source section’s B002 gloss covers disappearance. Those questioned about their former partners answer that they have gone away from them, a concrete case of what was relied on becoming absent.

The source section names “losing the way” as the root’s familiar sense. This verse says a person has ضَلَّ سَوَاءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ, a specific departure from the middle path that preserves the root’s path sense beside its hiddenness sense.
The source section names straying from the way as the root’s familiar sense. Here those making false comparisons are lost and cannot find a way, making the loss a failure to locate a path.

The section notes the root’s path-lost sense beside its “hidden and gone” sense. This verse says the Prophet’s companion has neither strayed nor erred, setting a clear boundary against reading 93:7 as moral deviation.

The section cites people asking whether they will be created anew after disappearing into the earth. This verse repeats the resurrection denial in different words: after being torn apart, they ask whether they will be in a new creation.
The verse asks whether people will return after dying and becoming dust. Like the section’s 32:10 example, bodily disappearance into earth is used to challenge resurrection.

The verse answers the disappearance claim by saying God knows what the earth diminishes of them and has a preserving record. It adds the counterpoint that what is hidden from human view is not lost to God.
The section describes what is hidden under a covering. This verse says the earth brings out its burdens, turning burial into visible emergence.
The verse explains that the earth reports because its Lord inspires it. This completes 99:4 by naming divine inspiration as the source of the ground’s disclosure.
The earth casts out what is within it and empties itself, a direct counterpart to the section’s hidden material becoming exposed.
The neighboring verse says the earth listens to and obeys its Lord. It completes the image of its disclosure with the source of its response.
The verse says graves are overturned, exposing what they held. This is a direct scene of what was covered in burial being brought into view.
The next verse says each soul will know what it sent ahead and left behind, completing the grave-opening scene with disclosure of its record.
The verse describes what is in the graves being scattered out, a direct image of buried contents becoming exposed.
The next verse says what is within breasts is brought out, extending the disclosure from graves to the hidden interior.
The verse says the cover is removed and sight becomes sharp. It directly joins uncovering to recovered vision, matching the section’s hidden-to-found movement.
The section centers what is concealed becoming known. This verse says hidden things will be tested or exposed, making disclosure itself the event of judgment.

The section’s water-in-milk dictionary image describes something present but obscured through mixture. This verse forbids mixing truth with falsehood and concealing truth, showing the moral cost of a mixture that hides what is true.
This verse repeats the warning not to clothe truth with falsehood or conceal it. It is a second direct formulation of the mixture-and-hiddenness relation in 2:42.
The section says the favor will no longer remain under cover but be told. This verse condemns concealing clear proofs and guidance after they have been made clear, a direct reversal of disclosure.
The following verse describes those who repent, repair, and make clear what was concealed. It completes 2:159 with the return from hiddenness to explicit explanation.
The verse recounts a covenant to make scripture clear to people and not conceal it, then says they cast it behind their backs. It closely stages the choice between disclosure and concealment.
The verse says the Messenger makes clear much of what the People of the Book had hidden from scripture. It gives the section’s covered-to-revealed movement a concrete scriptural scene.

The section says the Lord’s favor should be spoken openly. This verse says open charity is good while concealing it and giving it to the poor is better, setting a specific boundary on when a gift is shown.

The section urges naming the Lord’s favor. This town receives abundant provision from every direction but denies God’s blessings and is made to taste hunger and fear, showing the consequence of refusing to acknowledge favor.
The source section’s surah foundations include تَنْهَرْ, not to rebuff the petitioner. This verse uses the same Quranic command toward parents, forbidding harsh rebuff and requiring gracious speech.

The source section includes the orphan and the petitioner among the surah’s surrounding acts of care. This covenant likewise joins kindness to orphans with speaking well to people, including the way one addresses the vulnerable.

The source section’s surah context says not to oppress the orphan. This verse names the opposite act, repelling the orphan, as a sign of denying judgment, making care for the found and sheltered person a moral boundary.

The source section gives ح د ث a sense of bringing out and describes counsel as polishing hearts. This verse calls revelation أَحْسَنَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ and says it makes hearts soften at remembrance, a direct meeting of the word’s speech sense with its effect on the heart.

The source section says the hadith root can describe polishing a heart with admonitions. This verse says deeds have rusted over hearts, the contrary condition that makes the image of polishing perceptible.

The source section defines حديث as speech that reaches through hearing or revelation. This narrative begins by asking whether the report of Moses has reached the listener, then recounts a scene of divine address.

The source section describes speech as what reaches a hearer. This verse opens by asking whether the account of the overwhelming event has reached the Prophet, moving an unseen future event into recitation.

The section makes night a cover and daylight an opening, then moves from what is hidden to what is said. This verse puts concealed speech and public speech beside someone hidden by night and conspicuous by day, showing that both sides of the image are known to God.

The source section says words reach people by hearing or revelation and describes what is covered. This verse says that even speech made aloud leaves a secret and what is still more hidden, setting a limit on what public telling can expose.

The section describes blessings as both apparent and hidden. This verse applies the paired terms to God as the Manifest and the Hidden, shifting the visible/hidden distinction from the gift to its giver.

The section’s closing command concerns the favor of the Lord. This verse states that every blessing people have is from Allah, making explicit the attribution that the section asks its reader to voice.

The section moves from night and day to telling the Lord’s favor. This verse joins night and day with giving both secretly and publicly, a concrete parallel between hidden and open acts of generosity.
The verse describes punishment reaching towns at night or while their people rest at midday. It places the section’s two covered and exposed times in one scene of unexpected disclosure.
The verse asks whether a town feels secure from punishment arriving at night while its people sleep. It gives the hidden, sleeping side of the section’s night/day contrast.
The next verse asks whether a town feels secure from punishment arriving at duha while its people play. It supplies the exposed daylight counterpart to the sleeping night in 7:97.
The verse describes dawn being split, night as repose, and the sun and moon as measures. It makes the cover-to-day transition a created order, not just a shift in visibility.

The verse says God covers day with night as it pursues it, and names the sun, moon, and stars as subject to command. This repeats the section’s covering image in a larger account of the alternation of night and day.
The verse asks whether people see that night was made for rest and day for sight. It repeats the section’s contrast between what is hidden in night and what becomes visible by day.
The section calls night a covering beneath which things are unseen. These youths are made to sleep in a cave for years, a specific concealment that precedes their awakening.

The next verse says God awakens them so they may learn which group can best estimate how long they remained. It completes the concealment with a return to awareness and an attempt to name what passed unseen.

The section joins the night cover, exposure to the sun, and being guided or lost. This verse describes the sun turning away from the cave’s people and ends by distinguishing whom God guides from whom He leaves astray.
The youths seem awake though they are sleeping, and their dog lies at the cave entrance. This is a specific difference between what sight suggests and what remains hidden within the cave.

The youths awaken, ask one another how long they have remained, and send one to the city for food while urging discretion. It joins finding provision with the need to keep their hidden state from being exposed.
The youths fear being discovered and forced back into their former religion. This completes their concealment scene by naming what exposure would mean for them.

The source section’s dictionary gloss calls a town’s outward side its exposed edge. A man runs from the far end of Moses’s city with a warning, a specific scene of a voice emerging from the city’s edge into public view.

The source section’s dictionary gloss describes the exposed side of a town; the connection here is spatial rather than lexical. A man comes running from the farthest part of the city to urge his people to follow the messengers, so the city edge becomes the point from which a public message emerges.
The section describes وَجَدَ as noticing through perception. Moses finds two women holding their flock back from the watering crowd, notices their need, and asks what is happening.
After Moses waters their flock, he withdraws to shade and asks his Lord for whatever good He sends. The continuation connects a found need and a response with asking for provision.

A woman comes to Moses with her father’s invitation and the offer of a reward for watering the flock. The good deed that began with noticing need is made known through a spoken message and returned provision.

The section imagines someone hidden in a crowd and found at a glance. This verse describes needy people who appear self-sufficient but are recognized by their marks, making concealed need perceptible without an insistent request.
The section’s surrounding surah says not to rebuff the asker. This verse states that a due share of wealth belongs to the asker and the deprived, turning hidden generosity into an explicit right.
The verse says that the faithful keep a known share in their wealth, a detail that makes provision answerable to people in need rather than remaining solely with its holder.
The next verse identifies the recipients as the asker and the deprived, directly connecting the section’s treatment of a petitioner with a claim on provision.

The section describes finding by the senses and reason and moving from concealment to what is exposed. In Joseph’s story, his master is found at the door after a hidden encounter, and the woman’s torn shirt becomes visible evidence.
The verse introduces a witness who says to inspect which side of Joseph’s shirt is torn. It supplies the reasoning test that can turn a concealed event into a known one.
The witness says a tear from behind would show the woman’s accusation is false. This verse gives the physical criterion by which the hidden event can be judged.
The master sees the shirt torn from behind and recognizes the deception. This completes the passage from hidden action to evidence found and then interpreted.

The section uses water disappearing into milk as an image of something present but unseen within another substance. This verse describes pure milk emerging from within the animal, a related but distinct image of a drink whose origin lies hidden inside.

The section labels ض ل ل branch B004 with the dictionary sense “forget.” Moses asks not to be taken to task for what he forgot, a direct example of memory failing in the same narrative as the lost fish.
The section connects disappearance with forgetting and gives 2:282 as its example. This prayer asks not to be held accountable if people forget or err, making forgetfulness a named human limit.
The section’s secondary sense of ض ل ل is forgetting. This verse says Adam had previously been given a command but forgot it, showing a forgotten instruction rather than a lost path.

The section cites deniers who ask how people can be created anew after disappearing into the earth. This verse stages a person’s death for a century and return to life, with his food and drink preserved and his donkey restored, as a concrete answer to that denial.

The section reports denial of resurrection after bodily disappearance. Abraham asks how God gives life to the dead, and is shown birds gathered back after being placed on separate hills, a specific reversal of disintegration.
The verse repeats the question whether people will be raised in a new creation after becoming bones and fragments, another formulation of the section’s cited denial after disappearance.
The verse asks whether people will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones. It repeats the same bodily-disappearance challenge as the section’s 32:10 passage.
The verse asks whether people will be resurrected after they die and become dust and bones, a further direct formulation of the denial the section quotes.
The verse quotes people asking whether they will be resurrected after dying and becoming dust and bones. It repeats the same challenge while placing it in a passage that answers it.
The verse asks who can revive bones after they have decayed. It makes the bodily disappearance in the section’s resurrection example a specific image of bones losing their form.
The answer is that the One who created the bones the first time will revive them. This completes the challenge in 36:78 with the reversal from decay to restoration.

The source section describes words of admonition polishing the heart. This verse says that when God is mentioned hearts tremble and faith increases when His verses are recited, a specific response to heard revelation.

The section’s hadith gloss includes counseling hearts until they are polished. This verse asks whether believers’ hearts have become humble to God’s remembrance and revealed truth, contrasting a softened heart with one that has grown hard.

The source section’s sword and heart-polishing image implies cleansing what has accumulated. This verse says the person who purifies the soul succeeds, giving purification a concrete spiritual outcome.
The next verse says the person who buries or corrupts the soul fails. It supplies the direct opposite of purification and echoes the section’s hidden-versus-brought-into-view boundary.
The same Lord addresses the Prophet and says that He raised his mention. This is a specific public-mention counterpart to the section’s command that the Prophet tell of his Lord’s favor.

The verse says that Moses brought a scripture which people display on pages while concealing much of it. This is a concrete scriptural instance of the section’s movement between what is hidden and what is shown.

The source section defines حديث as speech that reaches a hearer. This verse says the disbelievers will wish the earth were leveled with them but will be unable to conceal any حديث from God, joining speech to the limit of concealment.

The source section says speech received through revelation is called حديث. This verse identifies the recited signs as God’s and asks what discourse people will believe after His signs, tying revelation to a hearer’s response.

The source section defines حديث as speech that reaches people and is then recounted. This verse calls the Quran “this discourse” and addresses the Prophet’s grief if people do not believe it, showing the consequence of a message reaching an unreceptive audience.

On the Day of Judgment, people’s hearing, sight, and skins testify against them. This is a specific reversal of the section’s movement from hidden experience to spoken account: the body itself discloses what its owner concealed.
The people ask their skins why they testified, and the skins answer that God made them speak. This completes 41:20 by naming the source of the disclosure.
The verse says that mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what people did. It is a specific image of hidden deeds becoming a spoken record.
The verse says that tongues, hands, and feet will testify to what people did. It repeats the body-as-witness image and makes private actions publicly known.
Each person arrives with a driver and a witness. This verse sets up the judgment scene that continues with the cover removed and sight made sharp in 50:22.
The verse says the written records are spread open. It gives a concrete disclosure of what had been preserved out of sight.
The next verse says each soul will know what it has brought. This completes the opened-record scene with recognition of what was hidden in one’s own deeds.
